expected_text_segments:
Update: The Fed held on October 28. Both dissenters wanted a hike.

The Fed's October 28 hold was a 10-2 decision. Both dissenters wanted higher rates.

What to watch: The next useful question is whether a later Committee decision changes the target range or the direction of the recorded vote. The October 28 documents should be read as that meeting's decision and implementation instructions, rather than a prediction of what comes next.

Read the full brief: https://capitalchronicle.substack.com/p/the-fed-held-on-october-28-both-dissenters

Retrospective analysis, written on 1 November 2026 (GMT+7) Analysis, not financial advice. Readers decide whether to trade.

media_manifest.alt_text: October 28, 2026 FOMC vote: 10 members approved holding the target range; 2 members, Lisa D. Cook and Beth M. Hammack, preferred a quarter-percentage-point increase. Horizontal member-count axis starts at zero.
media_manifest.attribution: Source: Federal Reserve Board, October 28, 2026 FOMC statement.
media_manifest.caption: The October 28 vote: 10 members approved a hold; Lisa D. Cook and Beth M. Hammack preferred a quarter-point increase. Sources: [Federal Reserve Board](https://www.federalreserve.gov/newsevents/pressreleases/monetary20261028a.htm).

September CPI: why 0.6% and 3.7% answer different questions

September CPI retrospective: the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics' October 14, 2026 release has monthly and annual readings.

Why it matters: Monthly and twelve-month readings in the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics' October 14, 2026 release on September CPI have different horizons and adjustment bases. Comparing 0.6% with 3.7% as competing answers would confuse those distinctions.

Read the full brief: https://capitalchronicle.substack.com/p/september-cpi-why-06-and-37-answer

Analysis, not financial advice. Readers decide whether to trade.

media_manifest.attribution: Source: BLS dated CPI releases. First readings; October 2025 not published.
media_manifest.caption: U.S. CPI-U, twelve-month change, not seasonally adjusted, October 2024-September 2026. Each point uses its first published reading. October 2025 has no published reading. Source: BLS dated CPI releases.

expected_text_segments:
September CPI: why 0.6% and 3.7% answer different questions

Why it matters: Monthly and twelve-month readings in the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics' October 14, 2026 release on September CPI have different horizons and adjustment bases. Comparing 0.6% with 3.7% as competing answers would confuse those distinctions.

Context: The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics' September CPI release of October 14, 2026 showed a lower monthly reading excluding food and energy. Giving that narrower measure more weight is an analytical choice, not proof that the all-items increase was temporary. Giving the headline more weight does not establish persistence either.

Read the full brief: https://capitalchronicle.substack.com/p/september-cpi-why-06-and-37-answer

Analysis, not financial advice. Readers decide whether to trade.
